title: Introduction to the Epistle of Jude
subtitle: A concise guide to the writer, setting, readers, false teachers, and enduring message of the brief letter that calls the church to contend for the faith.

blocks.text: The letter opens with a modest self-description: Jude names himself a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James. He offers no apostolic title, no list of credentials, and no account of how he came to faith. That restraint is itself telling. A writer who could identify himself simply by naming his brother must have been addressing believers who knew exactly which James was meant, and only one James in the early church was prominent enough to need no further description: the leader of the Jerusalem congregation who was also a brother of the Lord.

Several men called Judas appear in the New Testament, including Judas Iscariot, the other disciple of that name who asked Jesus a question in the upper room, Judas of Galilee who led a revolt, and Judas Barsabbas who carried the Jerusalem council’s decision to Antioch. None of these is ever linked with a well-known James. The Gospels, however, list Judas among the brothers of Jesus, together with James, Joses, and Simon. The most natural reading of the opening verse is that the writer is this Judas, the younger brother of James and therefore a member of the household of Nazareth.

The English form Jude is simply a convenient way of distinguishing him from the betrayer, since the Greek name is the same. The name itself carried honor in Jewish families, recalling the patriarch Judah and the Maccabean hero Judas, so it is not surprising that the family of Joseph and Mary chose it. Nothing in the letter’s contents argues against such a writer. Its vocabulary is that of someone at home in the Greek Scriptures, while its habits of thought, its love of examples from Israel’s history, and its familiarity with Jewish traditions about Enoch and Moses fit a believer raised in a devout Galilean home.

Some have suggested that a later admirer borrowed Jude’s name to give a message weight. Yet a forger seeking authority would hardly choose so obscure a figure, and would almost certainly have made more of the family tie with Jesus. The quiet phrasing of the opening, the absence of any claim to be an apostle, and the reference in verse 17 to the apostles as a group to which the writer does not belong all suit a genuine letter from the Lord’s brother. The early church received it slowly, chiefly because of its brevity and its use of Enoch, yet it was widely read and honored as Scripture.

The letter gives no direct statement of when or where it was written, so any date must be inferred. Jude writes as one who remembers the apostolic warnings about scoffers in the last time, which suggests that the apostles’ teaching was well established and that some of them had already finished their work. At the same time nothing in the letter hints that Jerusalem has fallen, and the writer appears to be a man of active ministry rather than an aged survivor of a distant era.

The close relationship between Jude and the second chapter of 2 Peter bears on the question. If Jude wrote first and Peter later drew on his material, the letter must be earlier than the apostle’s death, probably around A.D. 67, which would place it in the late 50s or the 60s. If Jude instead drew on 2 Peter, it could belong somewhere between A.D. 70 and 85. The evidence on either side is not decisive. A date in the 60s fits the picture of a brother of Jesus still active in the church, but the message does not depend on settling the year.

The place of writing is equally uncertain. Jude probably spent much of his life in Palestine, and Paul mentions that the brothers of the Lord travelled in missionary service, often accompanied by their wives. Jude may therefore have written from Judea or Galilee, or from somewhere along the routes his ministry took him. The readers seem to have lived in a setting where Jewish tradition was familiar and where Greek was the shared language, conditions found across Syria, Asia Minor, and many Mediterranean cities with Jewish-Christian communities.

The broader setting is a church in its second generation. The first preaching of the gospel had already gathered congregations, and the faith had been handed over as a recognized body of teaching. Now the danger came less from outward persecution than from inner corruption. Travelling teachers could move from city to city, receive hospitality, and speak at shared meals before their character became known. Jude writes into that vulnerable moment, when the church needed to distinguish faithful messengers from people who used grace as an excuse for license.

Jude addresses his readers broadly as those who are called, loved by God the Father, and kept for Jesus Christ. For this reason the letter has long been grouped with the general epistles, sent to believers rather than to a named city. Yet the warmth of the address and the specific danger described show that Jude had a real community or circle of congregations in mind. He calls them beloved repeatedly and speaks as a pastor who knows both their faith and their peril.

The readers were evidently well instructed in the Old Testament and in the Jewish traditions that grew up around it. Jude can mention the wilderness generation, the angels who left their proper dwelling, Sodom and Gomorrah, Cain, Balaam, and Korah without explaining any of them. He expects his audience to recognize allusions to Enoch’s prophecy and to the account of Michael and the devil. Such shorthand works only with people who had heard these stories from childhood or had been carefully taught them in the church, which points to a congregation with strong Jewish-Christian roots, though Gentile believers may well have shared in it.

Their world was shaped by the movement of people and ideas across the Roman Empire. Believers met in homes and gathered for shared meals that joined fellowship with the Lord’s Supper. Hospitality toward travelling ministers was a Christian duty, yet it also left an opening for impostors. Surrounding pagan culture treated sexual freedom as ordinary, and some within the church were tempted to think that grace released them from moral restraint. The pressure Jude addresses was therefore both doctrinal and practical, touching what believers confessed and how they lived.

Jude never suggests that the readers had already abandoned the faith. Rather, some among them were wavering, others had been drawn close to the danger, and a few were already caught in it. The letter treats the faithful as people able to help the doubting, to rescue those near the fire, and to show mercy with holy caution. It assumes a church that could still be strengthened and that bore real responsibility for its weaker members.

sections.title: Jude and the Family of Jesus

blocks.text: Jude grew up in the household of Nazareth with Jesus, James, Joses, Simon, and sisters whose names the Gospels do not record. The precise family relationship has been understood in more than one way. Many have taken these brothers to be younger sons of Joseph and Mary; others have regarded them as sons of Joseph by an earlier marriage or as close cousins. The Gospels call them brothers without qualification, and in any case Jude knew Jesus from the ordinary closeness of family life, sharing meals, labor, and the rhythms of village worship.

That nearness did not produce early faith. During the Galilean ministry the brothers of Jesus did not believe in Him, and on one occasion they urged Him to display His works publicly in Jerusalem. Their unbelief makes the later change all the more striking. After the resurrection, Jesus appeared to James, and by the time the disciples gathered in the upper room before Pentecost the brothers of the Lord were among them, joined in prayer with Mary and the apostles. Jude’s faith was born, not from family pride, but from the risen Christ.

This history explains the tone of the letter’s opening. Jude could have presented himself as the Lord’s brother and claimed a unique standing, yet he chose to be known as Christ’s servant. He had learned that physical kinship with Jesus counted for nothing apart from submission to Him as Lord. His reference to James likewise points away from himself, placing him beside a respected leader whose faithful service was well known. Humility, not privilege, frames everything that follows.

Later memory of the family adds a few details. A second-century tradition tells that two grandsons of Jude, poor farmers in Palestine, were brought before the emperor Domitian because they descended from David. When the emperor saw their work-hardened hands and heard that Christ’s kingdom was heavenly rather than political, he released them, and they became honored leaders in the churches. The story suggests that Jude’s household remained faithful and humble, and that his family continued to serve the church long after his own ministry ended.

events.title: Childhood in Nazareth
events.description: Jude grows up in the household of Joseph and Mary as one of the brothers of Jesus, alongside James, Joses, and Simon.

events.title: Unbelief During the Ministry
events.description: While Jesus preaches and heals in Galilee, His brothers remain unconvinced and question His public mission.

events.title: Resurrection and Faith
events.description: The risen Christ appears to James, and the brothers of the Lord join the disciples in prayer before Pentecost.

events.title: Service in the Early Church
events.description: James becomes a leading figure in Jerusalem while the Lord’s brothers take part in the growing work of the church.

events.title: Travelling Ministry
events.description: Paul refers to the brothers of the Lord as travelling missionaries who were accompanied by believing wives.

events.title: The Letter Is Written
events.description: Jude sets aside a planned letter on the shared salvation and urgently warns the church about ungodly intruders.

events.title: Jude’s Grandsons
events.description: Tradition remembers two of Jude’s grandsons as humble farmers questioned by Domitian and later honored in the churches.

blocks.text: Jude describes the troublemakers as certain people who had slipped in unnoticed. They were not outsiders attacking the church from beyond its walls, but participants within its fellowship who shared its meals and spoke in its gatherings. Their entrance was stealthy, and their true character became visible only gradually. Jude calls them ungodly, a word that captures the heart of the problem: they lived without reverence for God while still claiming a place among His people.

Their central error was to turn the grace of God into an excuse for immorality. They treated forgiveness as permission rather than as power for a changed life. Jude links this moral corruption with a doctrinal denial, for by their conduct they rejected Jesus Christ as the only Master and Lord. Whatever they confessed with their lips, their lives refused His authority. They defiled the body, rejected lawful authority, and spoke with contempt about spiritual realities they did not understand, relying on dreams or visions to justify their behavior.

Jude also exposes their influence within the congregation. They were like hidden reefs at the love feasts, ready to wreck anyone who drew too near. They shepherded only themselves, flattered people for advantage, grumbled against God’s ways, and followed their own desires. Their speech was loud and boastful, yet their lives produced nothing of lasting value. The vivid images of waterless clouds, fruitless trees, wild waves, and wandering stars show people who promised much and delivered nothing.

Most seriously, these teachers created division. They set themselves apart as spiritually superior while lacking the Spirit altogether. Jude does not provide a full description of their system, and attempts to name them as a known movement of the period remain uncertain. What matters is the pattern: a teaching that loosens the bond between grace and obedience, puts personal desire above Christ’s lordship, and divides the church while claiming higher insight. Such a pattern has reappeared in every age, which gives Jude’s warning enduring relevance.

sections.title: Jude’s Use of Scripture and Tradition

blocks.text: For so short a letter, Jude is dense with references to Israel’s history. He recalls the people delivered from Egypt who later perished in unbelief, the angels who abandoned their proper position, and the cities of the plain destroyed by fire. He then names Cain, Balaam, and Korah as patterns of rebellion. Each example shows that privilege does not protect those who turn from God, and that divine judgment, though delayed, is certain. Jude reads these stories as prophetic types that find their counterpart in the intruders of his own day.

The letter moves in a careful rhythm between ancient example and present application. Jude introduces a text or event, then turns with a phrase such as these are to show how it describes the false teachers. This pattern resembles the way Jewish teachers commented on Scripture, setting a passage beside its fulfillment. The structure reveals a writer who is not merely angry but thoughtful, building a case from the authority of the Word and inviting his readers to recognize the familiar shape of rebellion.

Jude also draws on traditions known among Jewish readers outside the Old Testament. In verse 9 he mentions that Michael the archangel contended with the devil about the body of Moses. Scripture records only that the Lord buried Moses in an unknown grave, yet Moses later appeared with Elijah on the mount of transfiguration, which points to his resurrection. Understood in the light of Daniel, Thessalonians, and the voice that raises the dead, Michael, the chief of the angels, is best identified with Christ Himself, who alone holds authority over death and who rebuked Satan by appealing to the Lord rather than by railing.

In verses 14 and 15 Jude quotes a prophecy attributed to Enoch, the seventh from Adam, foretelling the Lord’s coming with myriads of His holy ones to judge the ungodly. A similar statement appears in the Jewish writing known as 1 Enoch, which circulated widely in Jude’s time. Quoting a true statement does not endorse a whole book as Scripture, any more than Paul’s quotations of Greek poets endorse their writings. Guided by the Spirit, Jude recognized that this particular prophecy was true and used it to confirm what the rest of Scripture teaches about the Second Coming and the final judgment.

Jude explains his purpose with unusual candor. He had been eager to write about the salvation he and his readers shared, but news of the danger compelled him to change his plan. Instead he urged them to contend earnestly for the faith once for all delivered to the saints. That faith is the apostolic gospel, a settled body of truth given by God and entrusted to the church. It needed no revision, only faithful defense against those who would twist it into something else.

The letter therefore aims first to expose the intruders and to show their place in God’s moral order. By setting them beside the rebels of earlier ages, Jude assures his readers that the false teachers had not escaped God’s notice. Their condemnation had been foretold long before. The examples of judgment are sober warnings rather than threats of endless torment. Sodom and Gomorrah suffered the punishment of eternal fire in the sense that their destruction was complete and permanent; those cities no longer burn. In the same way the final end of the ungodly will be total and irreversible.

Jude’s deeper purpose is pastoral. After the warnings he turns to the beloved and urges them to build themselves up in their most holy faith, to pray in the Holy Spirit, to keep themselves in the love of God, and to wait for the mercy of the Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life. He calls them to show compassion to the doubting, to snatch some from the fire, and to show mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by sin. Defense of the truth must be joined with active love for people at risk.

The closing doxology gathers the whole message into praise. God alone is able to keep His people from falling and to present them faultless before His glory with exceeding joy. The contest for the faith is real, but the final security of believers rests on divine keeping power rather than human strength. Jude ends by giving glory, majesty, dominion, and power to the only God our Saviour through Jesus Christ, before all time, now, and forever, leaving his readers with confidence rather than fear.

Jude belongs among the shortest books of the New Testament, yet it carries the force of a prophetic warning. Its twenty-five verses move from greeting and purpose to a series of examples from Scripture and tradition, then to a vivid exposure of the intruders, and finally to exhortation and praise. The letter shows that faithful Christianity requires both clear conviction and practical love, and that the church must guard what God has entrusted to it.

Much of Jude’s material appears in a similar form in the second chapter of 2 Peter, where many of the same examples and images describe false teachers. The two letters differ in emphasis. Peter speaks of such teachers as coming in the future, while Jude sees them already at work. Peter adds the flood and the rescue of Noah and Lot, while Jude includes Cain, Korah, Michael, and Enoch. Read together, they show two servants of Christ confronting the same danger with complementary emphases.

blocks.title: Letter at a Glance
rows: Author
Jude, servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, best understood as one of the brothers of the Lord
Date
Uncertain; probably the A.D. 60s if written before 2 Peter, possibly A.D. 70–85 if written after it
Place of writing
Unknown; possibly Palestine or a place along the routes of Jude’s travelling ministry
Original readers
Believers familiar with the Old Testament and Jewish tradition, probably congregations with strong Jewish-Christian roots
Occasion
Ungodly intruders had slipped into the fellowship, turning grace into license and denying Christ’s lordship by their conduct
Key verse
Jude 1:3, the call to contend earnestly for the faith once for all delivered to the saints
Central message
God judges those who corrupt His grace, yet He keeps His people and presents them faultless before His glory
Structure
Greeting, purpose, examples of judgment, exposure of the intruders, apostolic warning, exhortation, and doxology
Distinctive features
Rich use of Old Testament types, groups of three, the dispute over Moses’ body, and the prophecy of Enoch

blocks.title: Jude and 2 Peter Compared
rows: Timing of the danger
False teachers have already crept into the fellowship
False teachers will arise among the believers in the future
Examples of judgment
Israel in the wilderness, rebellious angels, Sodom and Gomorrah, Cain, Balaam, and Korah
Rebellious angels, the flood, Sodom and Gomorrah, and Balaam, with Noah and Lot as examples of rescue
Use of tradition
Refers to Michael and the body of Moses and quotes the prophecy of Enoch
Speaks of angels generally without naming Michael or quoting Enoch
Second Coming
Briefly affirmed through Enoch’s prophecy of the Lord’s coming in judgment
Developed at length in answer to scoffers who deny His return
Closing emphasis
God’s power to keep believers from falling and present them faultless
Growth in the grace and knowledge of the Lord Jesus Christ
